title: Shishupala
hook: the rite needs someone to receive the first honor, Bhishma names Krishna, and the king of Chedi stands up
carry: wait one breath before you say anything

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rajasuya: Duryodhana receiving the gifts, Krishna washing the guests' feet. Your line was where you stand changes what you see. Did you take a quiet job no one asked you to do? Day seven hundred fifty-eight.
screen: `WHERE YOU STAND CHANGES WHAT YOU SEE.`

segments.voice: Who gets served first? It sounds small until you're the host: the seating plan, the first plate, the toast. At Yudhishthira's great rite, the question has a name. The custom is to offer an honored guest the arghya, a respectful welcome of water and gifts. And one guest must receive it first, before all the others. The hall is full of kings, elders, teachers and priests. Whoever is chosen, someone else is not. Today Yudhishthira asks the question, and we meet the man who will not accept the answer.
screen: `WHO IS SERVED FIRST?` → `THE ARGHYA: THE GUEST'S WELCOME.` → `ONE CHOSEN, MANY NOT.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira turns to the eldest of the family, his grandfather Bhishma, and asks: who among these should receive the first honor? Bhishma doesn't name a king or a priest. He names Krishna. In the telling, he says that among all those gathered, Krishna shines like the sun among lights. So the youngest Pandava, Sahadeva, brings the arghya and offers it to Krishna, and Krishna accepts it. That should be the end of it. A choice made by the eldest, carried out by the host, received by the guest. But a voice rises from the crowd. It belongs to Shishupala, king of Chedi. And he is furious. Here's the first thing to know about him. He isn't a stranger. Shishupala is Krishna's cousin, the son of Krishna's father's sister. They're family, and the poem will tell us later that the bond between them runs strange and deep. Here's the second thing. Shishupala doesn't object quietly. He doesn't take Yudhishthira aside. He stands up in front of every king in the hall and makes his complaint as public as the honor was. That's what this week is about. An honor given in public, and an objection that refuses to stay small. The Rajasuya was a picture of everyone in their place. Now one man is saying, loudly, that the place is wrong. Over the next days we'll hear what he says, how the hall answers, and why Krishna waits as long as he does before he answers at all.
screen: `WHO GETS THE FIRST HONOR?` · `BHISHMA NAMES KRISHNA.` · `SAHADEVA OFFERS THE ARGHYA.` · `SHISHUPALA, KING OF CHEDI, STANDS.` · then, large: `AN HONOR GIVEN IN PUBLIC.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let the shoulders drop. Bring to mind a time when someone else was honored and you weren't: a promotion, a prize, a toast, a seat at the head of the table. You don't have to judge the feeling that comes, whatever it is. Just notice where it lives in the body: the jaw, the chest, the stomach. Breathe into that spot, slowly, a few times. If you pray, you can bring that moment into your prayer. If not, let the breath soften it a little. The bell holds the time.
Shishupala. King of Chedi, Krishna's cousin, the man who stands up when Krishna receives the first honor at the Rajasuya.
Your line: wait one breath before you say anything. Today, when someone else gets the credit, notice your first reaction, and wait one breath before you say anything. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Offering arghya, water and a respectful welcome to an honored guest or to a deity, is part of traditional Hindu hospitality and worship; at the Rajasuya, the Mahabharata turns the whole scene on who receives it first.

original.note: Sanskrit arghya: the respectful offering of water and gifts made to an honored guest.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king who interrupts a party.
what it means: Krishna's own cousin, objecting in public to the first honor given at the Rajasuya.
what a scholar hears: the objection is to a ritual choice made by the eldest and carried out by the host, so it challenges the whole rite, not only Krishna.
